title: Eating out — and an object marker English doesn't have
goal: Order food and drinks, read a menu — and use را, the one piece of Persian grammar with no counterpart at all in English.

notes: ⚠️ **The marker را flags a SPECIFIC object, and English has nothing quite like it.** Compare غذا می‌خورم ("I eat" — any food) with غذا **را** می‌خورم ("I eat the food" — the food we've been talking about). The difference is exactly "I'm buying a book" versus "I'm buying **the** book" — and that's the best handle you have: **را roughly does the job of "the" on an object**, except it comes after the noun.

**When را is required:** when the object has این or آن, is a name, has a possessive ending, or has already been mentioned. **When را is left out:** when the object is general and not specific. کتاب می‌خرم ("I buy books") — no را. کتاب **را** می‌خرم ("I buy the book") — with را.

**In speech it's رو (*ro*), or just an attached ـو.** منو رو بده (*meno ro bede*), اینو می‌خوام (*ino mikhâm*, from این را می‌خواهم). The short form is what you'll hear; full را is mostly what you'll read.

⚠️ **Iranian food is not spicy — which surprises many visitors.** The backbone of Iranian cooking is **sour** (dried limes, pomegranate, sour fruit) and **fragrant** (saffron, cinnamon, turmeric), not hot. If you can't eat without chili sauce, bring your own; فلفل (pepper) is on the table, but you won't find hot chilies in an Iranian kitchen.
***Nush-e jân!*** **(نوشِ جان) = "enjoy your meal"**, literally "a delight to the soul". Said by waiters, hosts, or anyone who sees you start eating. The reply: ممنون.

⚠️ **The phrase حساب با من است is not empty politeness.** In Iran, fighting over the bill is a national sport. Whoever invited usually really will pay, and refusing once or twice is part of the etiquette. If you truly want to pay, do it quietly before the bill arrives — that's the move that wins. The whole mechanism is taken apart in unit 15.

grammars.title: The marker را — for specific objects
body: Persian marks the direct object with را, but **only when the object is specific**. This is the one part of Persian grammar that feels truly foreign to English speakers, and mastering it takes weeks, not minutes.
after: **The marker را is required** when the object: has این or آن (این کتاب را), is a name (مریم را دیدم), has a possessive ending (کتابم را), or has been mentioned before.
**The marker را is not used** when the object is general, non-specific, or part of a compound verb: کار می‌کنم (not کار را می‌کنم), غذا می‌خورم, فارسی صحبت می‌کنم.
⚠️ **The marker را is only for direct objects.** If the noun has a preposition in front (به، از، با، در), را is not allowed: به مریم گفتم (not به مریم را گفتم).
With pronouns, را can merge into one word: من را → **مرا** (*marâ*), تو را → **ترا** or تو را, then او را, ما را, شما را, آنها را. In conversation they all use رو: منو، تورو، اونو.

grammars.title: Ordering and asking
after: ***Bedun-e*** **(بدونِ, "without")** is a key word for anyone with dietary needs: بدونِ گوشت، بدونِ پیاز، بدونِ شکر. For allergies: به ... حساسیت دارم (*be ... hassâsiyat dâram*, "I'm allergic to ...").

blocks.title: How Iranians drink tea
items: **Tea is drunk with no sugar in it.** A sugar lump (قند — the root of English *candy*) goes between your teeth, and you sip the tea through it. This is called چای قندپهلو (*châi ghand-pahlu*, "tea with sugar on the side"). The glass is small, clear, and narrow-waisted — an استکان (*estekân*).

⚠️ **Turning down the first glass of tea is normal; turning down the third needs words.** بس است، ممنون (*bas ast, mamnun*, "that's enough, thanks") or سیر شدم (*sir shodam*, "I'm full"). Covering the glass with your palm is understood everywhere too.

blocks.title: Four sentences that make a host happy
items: "Thank you for all your trouble." — دستتان درد نکند.
"I'm full, thank you." — سیر شدم، ممنون.
"How do you make this?" — این را چطور درست می‌کنید؟ This last one almost always earns you the full recipe, a second helping, and an invitation to come back.
